header:
Date: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dana Ruiz (Redwood SE), Jules Kwan (CTO, Mooring), Rafi Morales (Lead ML Eng), Ivy Chen (Infra), Trevor Ames (Product)
Meeting recorded via Fireflies.ai
summary: Discovery focused on Mooring Labs' p95 and throughput targets for a streaming conversational product. Discussed latency targets (target p95 200ms for token stream), concurrency expectations (200 concurrent streams with 1–2 KB prompt sizes), tradeoffs between Hosted/Dedicated/Private, KV cache cold starts and warm caching strategy, security requirements (SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS), and an agreed next step to run a one‑week dedicated trial with a Redwood benchmark harness using customer prompt sets.
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm lena from Redwood, i'll kick us off. quick roll call?
[00:12] Jules Kwan: Jules here, rafi, ivy and trevor are with me.
[00:16] Rafi Morales: hi all./sorry, muffled — we have a kid at home so —
[00:20] Samir Patel: no worries, great to meet you. so high level today we want to understand your p95 targets, concurrency and streaming profile and what hosting mode you're leaning toward.
[00:30] Trevor Ames: yes, we run a live chat assistant in our maritime telematics app, it's streaming real‑time to operators. target p95 is around 200ms per token for the streamed response, but we can tolerate up to 350ms for some bursts.
[00:43] Dana Ruiz: okay that helps. how big are the requests and typical token lengths?
[00:48] Rafi Morales: prompts are small — 80 to 300 tokens depending on diagnostic payloads, typical completions are 50–150 tokens. Our traffic pattern has steady daytime traffic plus bursts when a fleet event triggers simultaneous sessions. we forecast ~200 concurrent active streams at peak, but bursts to 600 for short windows (1–5 minutes).
[01:10] Lena Ortiz: excellent. and are you planning to stream token by token to clients (server‑side streaming) or prebuffer?
[01:16] Trevor Ames: token streaming to client, we need 1st token within 120–150ms ideally, then steady token emission.
[01:24] Samir Patel: got it. for streamed workloads, p95 per token is the right metric. can i ask what models you're evaluating — open models or commercial?
[01:31] Jules Kwan: mainly open — we're experimenting with 13B and 70B quantized variants. cost's a factor so quantized 70B or 13B with good prompt engineering.
[01:40] Samir Patel: okay. two obvious levers: batching and KV cache. for conversation style streaming we usually avoid large server batches because that adds tail latency. we rely on KV/prefix cache to reduce decode time and small, aggressive batching (10–50ms windows) to preserve latency.
[01:56] Rafi Morales: the KV cache — how cold‑start heavy is that? when a new user session starts we'll have cold keys.
[02:02] Dana Ruiz: right, so we typically see a cold start penalty when the KV isn't primed — on Redwood Dedicated/Private you can get priming strategies (prewarm common prefixes, keep warmed replicas) and caching across GPUs. Hosted has cache too but cross‑tenant warming is more conservative.
[02:20] Rafi Morales: numbers — any ballpark on cold versus warm per token p95?
[02:24] Samir Patel: warm token p95 for a quantized 13B on a current gen A100/80GB equivalent node can be ~80–120ms depending on sequence length; cold start can add 60–180ms (model load or KV miss). for 70B quantized on a bfloat node, warm maybe 150–250ms per token, cold could push above your 350ms threshold.
[02:45] Jules Kwan: okay so 70B is risky for our 200ms target. sounds like 13B quantized or a smaller model with more aggressive caching is the pragmatic path.
[02:55] Lena Ortiz: that matches what many customers choose — Dedicated gives you control to tune prewarming/replicas and predictable throughput. Hosted can still work but we'd recommend dedicated for your 200ms p95 target at scale.
[03:06] Ivy Chen: about dedicated — do you allow private VPC peering? we have strict egress and need KMS/HSM for keys.
[03:12] Samir Patel: yes Dedicated and Private both support VPC peering and bring‑your‑own KMS/HSM options. Private (on‑prem or customer VPC control plane) gives you full data plane isolation and we can integrate with your HSM. we also provide audit logs and SOC2 docs.
[03:28] Trevor Ames: network egress — what IP ranges do we need to open?
[03:32] Dana Ruiz: we'll send a concise allowlist. for the trial we'll give a reduced set and a temporary key/range.
[03:38] Rafi Morales: back on throughput — tokens/sec and concurrency. if we want 200 concurrent streams, each emitting ~5 tokens/sec, that's 1,000 tok/sec sustained; plus overhead for prompt decode and context. can your serving runtime hit that on a small pool?
[03:53] Samir Patel: yes depends on model and node type. for quantized 13B, a 4‑GPU pool can handle ~1k–2k tok/sec sustained with steady memory usage and concurrency shaping. for the bursts (600 sessions), we recommend autoscale/temporary burst nodes or reserved headroom.
[04:10] Lena Ortiz: we can model cost: reserved Dedicated capacity for baseline plus burst capacity for events. Our Optimize tool will suggest batching and cache configs to minimize unit price while meeting p95 targets.
[04:18] Jules Kwan: curious about streaming fairness — if lots of concurrent streams, do some streams starve?
[04:22] Samir Patel: we have scheduling policies: strict latency SLO routing (prioritize low latency streams), token quota-based multiplexing, and per‑customer weight. you can choose fairness or strict p95 SLO.
[04:34] Ivy Chen: do you support routing by region? we want EU data residency for EU fleets.
[04:38] Dana Ruiz: yes region routing is supported, and we can pin model variants per region. fallback policies let requests roll over to another region's compatible model if capacity is constrained but only if policy allows (data residency concerns noted).
[04:50] Rafi Morales: operationally, what does a benchmark run look like?
[04:54] Samir Patel: two parts: 1) a synthetic token‑level replay using your prompt/response shapes to measure warm/cold p95 and tokens/sec, 2) a live streaming run that opens N concurrent websocket/tcp streams and measures 1st token latency and sustained emission. we'll push a harness, and we'll run it against a Dedicated trial pool we provision for you.
[05:13] Trevor Ames: how long to spin that pool up?
[05:16] Dana Ruiz: for a trial we can provision within 24–48 hours for Dedicated in most regions; Private on‑prem takes longer (packaging/infra).
[05:24] Jules Kwan: security review — we need SOC2 TYPE II, SAML SSO, RBAC, BYOK.
[05:30] Lena Ortiz: we've got SOC2 reports and SAML integrations; we'll share the compliance pack. RBAC and audit logs are available on Dedicated/Private, and we support BYOK via KMS and HSM integration.
[05:40] Ivy Chen: also need retention controls and the ability to opt out of model telemetry for PII.
[05:44] Samir Patel: retention controls and telemetry opt‑out are supported at the tenant level on Dedicated and Private. Hosted customers may have more limited options depending on plan but we can discuss specifics in the security packet.
[05:55] Rafi Morales: pricing sensitivity — we can't blow the budget. can you ballpark relative cost of hosted vs dedicated?
[05:59] Lena Ortiz: hosted is simpler and has lower upfront but higher marginal cost. Dedicated has monthly commit but lower per‑token unit cost. for sustained 1k tok/sec baseline Dedicated tends to be more economical at scale, especially with quantized models and cache.
[06:12] Trevor Ames: what's the pilot scope you propose?
[06:16] Lena Ortiz: 1 week Dedicated trial with a small reserved pool sized to your baseline (we recommend capacity for 300 concurrent with autoscale headroom to 700 for bursts). we'll run the synthetic and live streaming benchmarks with your prompt sets, collect p95 metrics, and iterate on caching/batching configs. Samir will run the harness and we'll provide results and optimization recommendations.
[06:33] Jules Kwan: sounds good. one thing — cold start during a simultaneous fleet event is our biggest risk. can you simulate that?
[06:39] Samir Patel: yes we'll run a cold‑start storm test that spins up many new sessions rapidly to measure model load and KV priming impact. we'll also measure model swap fallback latencies if we need to drop to a smaller variant during overload.
[06:51] Ivy Chen: please include details on IP allowlist and KMS endpoints in the security packet.
[06:55] Dana Ruiz: noted, we'll attach network diagram and KMS integration steps.
[06:59] Lena Ortiz: recap and next steps: I will send pricing and trial docs, Samir will drop the benchmark harness and a README with workload template, Ivy will share allowlist and SSO contact, and we'll schedule the trial week of 3/10. any other asks?
[07:15] Jules Kwan: please include an example cost model with numbers for 13B quantized vs 70B quantized.
[07:20] Lena Ortiz: will do.
[07:22] Rafi Morales: and include the test checklist for the cold start storm.
[07:25] Samir Patel: will include the checklist and scripts.
[07:28] Trevor Ames: thanks, that's helpful. we'll review the packet and lock a date later today.
[07:33] Lena Ortiz: thanks all, we'll follow up.
[07:36] Jules Kwan: thanks everyone.
[07:38] (recording ends)
